title: The 48-hour rule for things you did not plan to buy
description: Want something unplanned? Wait two days. Desire that survives 48 hours is information; desire that fades was just weather.

body.heading: Why waiting works
paragraphs: Shops are engineered to make wanting feel urgent: bright images, countdown timers, "only three left." The feeling is real, but it is about the moment, not the object. Two days later the moment has passed and you can judge the thing itself.
Forty-eight hours is long enough for the glow to fade and short enough that a genuine need is not harmed by the delay. If the item sells out meanwhile, you have lost a purchase, not a necessity.

body.heading: How to run the rule
paragraphs: When the urge strikes, note the item and its price, then set a reminder for two days later. Do not keep browsing the page in the meantime — that is just marinating in the advertisement.

When the reminder arrives, ask three questions: do I still want it, what would it replace, and which pot pays for it? Three clear yeses and the purchase is a decision. Anything fuzzy and the answer is not yet.

body.heading: Exceptions, honestly handled
paragraphs: The rule is for non-essentials. Replacing a broken kettle or buying medicine does not need a waiting period. And genuinely time-limited essentials — a train ticket you must have — are planned purchases, not impulses in disguise.

If you notice you keep granting yourself exceptions, tighten the paperwork rather than the willpower: write the item, the price, and the date the wait ends, every time. A rule you can see is a rule you can keep.

takeaway: Give every unplanned non-essential a 48-hour wait. What you still want after two days, you can buy with a clear head and a named pot.
